summary.oneLiner: Incorporated in 1939, The Ugar Sugar Works Ltd is one of the leading sugar factories in Karnataka, running an integrated sugar, industrial and potable alcohol, and bagasse-based cogeneration complex across two units.

currentContext.business: The Company is engaged in the manufacture and sale of sugar, industrial and potable alcohol, and the generation and distribution of electricity. Cane is crushed at its Ugar and Jewargi units in Karnataka, with molasses and byproducts routed into a distillery producing industrial alcohol (ethanol) and potable alcohol, and bagasse used to generate power. Sugar reaches households and institutional users through sugar agents, ethanol goes to oil marketing companies for blending, potable alcohol is sold as IML through the Karnataka State Beverages Corporation, and surplus power is sold on the exchange through PTC India Ltd.

currentContext.strengths: Integrated sugar-to-alcohol-to-power model: cane crushed at two units feeds a distillery producing industrial and potable alcohol while bagasse feeds cogeneration, diversifying away from sugar alone|Multiple independent offtake channels - sugar agents and institutional buyers, oil marketing companies for ethanol, KSBCL for potable alcohol, and the power exchange through PTC India Ltd|Long operating history since incorporation on 11-09-1939, presenting its 86th Annual Report, and described as one of the leading sugar factories in Karnataka|Cane-catchment and labour ecosystem support: a well-equipped township with clubhouse, playground and gymnasium plus a Cooperative Society, Hospital, School and College operated for workers and the general public|Promoter-led board with seven promoter directors alongside seven non-executive independent directors, and a proper and adequate system of internal control with an Internal Auditor covering almost all areas of operations
currentContext.strategies: Operate an integrated sugar-ethanol-cogeneration model across the two units at Ugar and Jewargi, with surplus power exported to the exchange through PTC India Ltd.|Maintain a proper and adequate system of internal control so that all assets are safeguarded and protected, with the Internal Auditor reporting on almost all areas of operations.|The Board has recommended a 10% dividend (Rs. 0.10 per share) for the year, against nil in the previous year, and no amount has been transferred to Reserve for FY 2025-26. Distributions are governed by a formal Dividend Distribution Policy formulated by the Board pursuant to Regulation 43A of the SEBI Listing Regulations, which is published on the Company's website. The BRSR confirms the Company has no holding, subsidiary, associate or joint-venture companies, so capital is deployed within the standalone entity; CSR is applicable to the Company under Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013. Governance philosophy frames capital stewardship as achieving long-term corporate goals, enhancing shareholders' value and attaining the highest level of transparency over a sustained period.|ISO 14001:2015 (environmental management) and ISO 9001:2015 (quality management) certifications adopted and mapped to the NGRBC principles.|Company states it is setting up guidelines and timelines for various compliances under Environmental, Social and Governance principles; management is in the process of setting specific goals - i.e. no defined-timeline ESG commitments or targets exist yet.|No periodic NGRBC review mechanism in place yet - the Company is in the process of finalising the structure for periodic review of the principles (both compliance with statutory requirements and performance against policies).|Board-approved policies cover all nine NGRBC principles and have been translated into procedures; the policy suite includes a Risk Management Policy, Vigil Mechanism, CSR Policy, Business Responsibility Policy and Dividend Distribution Policy, accessible at www.ugarsugar.com.|Policies do not yet extend to value chain partners; management states it is taking steps to extend certain policies to them.|No formal stakeholder grievance redressal mechanism - the company acknowledges issues raised by stakeholder groups are addressed from time to time rather than through a formal process; nil complaints reported across stakeholder groups.|Social infrastructure for workers and the surrounding public: a well-equipped township with clubhouse, playground and gymnasium, plus a Cooperative Society, Hospital, School and College; regular training and all-round exposure provided to employees.|Workforce diversity is low - females are 1.67% of total employees, 3.24% of total workers and 14.29% of the Board, with 0% female Key Managerial Personnel and no differently-abled employees or workers.|CSR is applicable under Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013.|Co-generation from bagasse is an operating sustainability lever - 1968.56 Lakh kW generated at Ugar and Jewargi during the year (vs 1471.30 Lakh prior year) with 763.96 Lakh kW exported to the exchange via PTC India Ltd; bagasse-based power is 2.13% of turnover.|Ethanol supply to the Ethanol Blending Programme aligns the company with India's 20% blending target; India achieved a 19.98% blending ratio in ESY 2026.
currentContext.expansion: The annual report discloses no new capex project, capacity addition, commissioning timeline or acquisition. Operations remain across the company's two existing units, Ugar and Jewargi, spanning sugar, co-generation (described as "Co-generation (Ugar & Jewargi)") and distillery output of industrial and potable alcohol/ethanol; surplus power is exported and supplied to the exchange through PTC India Ltd. The only expansion-adjacent capital disclosure is in the BRSR, where R&D and capital expenditure investments in specific technologies to improve environmental and social impacts of products and processes are reported as Nil for both FY 2025-26 and FY 2024-25. On ESG the company states it "is setting up guidelines and timeline for various compliances under Environmental, Social and Governance principles" and that "Management is in the process of setting specific goals", with no defined timeline given. Growth commentary in the MD&A is industry-level (national sugar production, ethanol blending, global balances) rather than company capacity plans; the company-level figures reported are utilisation/throughput outcomes for the year at the existing Ugar and Jewargi units.
currentContext.mdna: India's 2025-26 season has continued on a confident and encouraging note, supported by ample sugarcane availability, improved on-ground productivity and enhanced operational efficiency across key producing states.|SY2026 Indian sugar production rose 4.39% YoY to 30.90 million MT on adequate sugarcane availability and improved yield; Maharashtra leads mill operations, followed by Uttar Pradesh and Karnataka.|Total domestic availability of 33.00 million tonnes (including 5 million tonne opening stock) exceeds domestic consumption of 28.00 million tonnes, and ISO expects a global 2025/26 surplus of 1.625 million tonnes on higher production.|Planting for 2026-27 has improved in Maharashtra and Karnataka, promising ample opening stocks of 4.25 million tonnes.|Yield pressure is regional: Uttar Pradesh yields are lower due to a varietal replacement programme (though recovery rates improved), while Maharashtra and Karnataka saw reduced yields from early sugarcane flowering caused by excess rain and shorter harvest windows from higher crush rates.|The Government of India has continued the release mechanism for sale of sugar and maintained the minimum selling price at Rs.31/- per kg to control falling sugar prices.|Ethanol demand is a structural driver: India achieved a 19.98% blending ratio in ESY2026 with 239 crore litres blended, and Indian ethanol production surged to 10.5 bln litres from 7.34 bln litres as the country pivots to grain-based feedstocks (now over 60% of production) to meet its 20% blending target.|Global ethanol production is projected at 122.0 bln litres in 2025 (up 2.3%) with consumption at 121.7 bln litres (up 3.3%), aided by stronger offtake in India, Canada and Colombia, expanding European consumption on higher blending targets and E10 availability, and Vietnam/Indonesia preparing E10 and E5 mandates in 2026.|International sugar prices have declined substantially, with raw sugar at $313/MT in February 2026 versus $445/MT a year earlier and white sugar at $408/MT versus $532/MT; the white-raw premium widened to $95/MT from $87/MT.|Exports are unlikely to be a meaningful outlet: India is likely to ship only 7.5 to 8 lakh tonnes in the 2025-26 marketing season, well short of the quota made available, as weak global price parity discourages outbound sales.|Cane cost is rising: for SY2026 the FRP was increased by Rs.15 to Rs.355/quintal at a basic recovery of 10.25%, UP-SAP rose by Rs.30 to Rs.400/quintal (early maturing) and Rs.390/quintal (normal), and Karnataka SAP was increased by Rs.250/quintal during the year.

risks.note: BRSR flags cane as an integral and essential part of the manufacturing process whose timely availability depends on climate and other conditions like pricing; financial implication indicated as negative. Company states the risk is not under control and mitigates only by maintaining production and manufacture of other by-products.

risks.risk: Government policy changes, particularly on cane FRP and administered sugar pricing
risks.note: BRSR lists change in Government policies on FRP as a risk with negative financial implication; mitigation is to follow Government guidelines and focus on co-generation and by-products. MD&A adds that FRP rose Rs.15 to Rs.355/quintal for SY2026 (10.25% basic recovery) and Karnataka SAP rose Rs.250/quintal, while MSP has not been revised since 2019 (industry urging revision to Rs.39/kg) - a squeeze between rising input cost and a frozen output floor price.

risks.risk: Climate change and adverse weather affecting crop yield and quality
risks.note: BRSR environmental issues row: changes in rainfall patterns, temperatures and extreme weather events can affect crop yields and quality; negative financial implication. MD&A corroborates - Maharashtra and Karnataka saw reduced yields from early sugarcane flowering due to excess rain and shorter harvest windows.

risks.risk: Water availability / drought exposure at the plants
risks.note: BRSR: the company is situated on the banks of the Krishna River with the Hippergi barrage nearby and sufficient water is normally available, but in a drought situation there is a shortage of water. Mitigated through effective water management practices; financial implication negative.

risks.risk: Farmer engagement dependency for continuous cane supply
risks.note: BRSR: sugar production requires a timely and continuous supply of good quality cane which may be affected by improper farmer engagement. Mitigated through cordial relations with farmers and an R&D cell plus field staff visiting farmers for cultivation guidance and yield enhancement.

risks.risk: Labour practices, farm labour cost and attrition
risks.note: BRSR flags poor labour practices as a credibility and high-turnover risk with negative financial implication. MD&A adds that human labour constitutes 52% of total sugarcane cultivation cost, so any change flows directly into cost of cultivation; increased farm mechanisation is cited as the offset.

risks.risk: Regulatory/taxation risk on industrial alcohol after the Supreme Court ruling
risks.note: MD&A: in October 2024 the Supreme Court upheld States' power to regulate industrial alcohol, which may give state governments the ability to tax it. Material because Industrial Alcohol is the single largest revenue line at 44.66% of turnover.

risks.risk: Sugar oversupply and weak export parity
risks.note: MD&A: with 5 million tonne opening stock, total domestic availability of 33.00 million tonne exceeds consumption of 28.00 million tonne, and ISO expects a global surplus of 1.625 million tonnes for 2025/26. India is likely to ship only 7.5-8 lakh tonnes in the 2025-26 season, well short of the quota, as weak global price parity discourages outbound sales; international raw sugar fell to $313/MT in Feb 2026 from $445/MT a year earlier. The company itself did not export any sugar during the year and does not export directly.
